title: Topics
subtitle: Logical event categories backed by immutable, append-only distributed commit logs.
keyTakeaways: A Kafka topic is a logical category that clients produce to and consume from, physically realized as an ordered, immutable commit log.
Events in a topic are persistent and append-only: reading a message does not delete it, allowing multiple independent consumer groups to read at their own pace.
Topic granularity requires balance: creating one topic per entity type leads to thousands of idle partitions, while putting all events into one topic breaks schema safety.
architectureDiagram:
KAFKA TOPIC PHYSICAL LOG ANATOMY
Topic: "payment-events"
  +--- Partition 0: [ Offset 0 ][ Offset 1 ][ Offset 2 ][ Offset 3 ] ---> (Append-Only)
  +--- Partition 1: [ Offset 0 ][ Offset 1 ][ Offset 2 ] -------------> (Append-Only)
  +--- Partition 2: [ Offset 0 ][ Offset 1 ][ Offset 2 ][ Offset 3 ] ---> (Append-Only)

Multiple Independent Consumers (Zero Destructive Reads):
  Consumer Group A (Fraud Detection) -> Reading Partition 0 at Offset 3
  Consumer Group B (Audit Ledger)    -> Reading Partition 0 at Offset 1 (Replaying)

sections.heading: Logical Abstraction Over Distributed Commit Logs
sections.body: In traditional message brokers like RabbitMQ, messages are transient: once a consumer acknowledges a message, the broker deletes it from memory or disk. Kafka inverts this model. A topic is a durable, ordered, append-only log. Writers append records to the end of the log; readers retain their own offset pointers and scan forward through the log without mutating it. This allows dozens of independent consumer services to read the exact same event stream without interfering with each other.
bullets: Immutable Retention: Records remain stored on disk for a configured retention period (e.g., 7 days or 1 TB), regardless of whether they have been read.
Sequential Disk I/O: Appending sequentially to the end of an OS file allows modern NVMe and HDD disks to operate at raw physical bandwidth limits, avoiding random disk seeks.
Kernel Zero-Copy (sendfile): Kafka serves consumer reads directly from the OS page cache to the network socket using the `sendfile` syscall, completely bypassing user-space memory copies.

sections.heading: Topic Taxonomy and Schema Governance
sections.body: A common architecture dilemma is deciding topic granularity: should you create fine-grained topics (`user-created`, `user-email-updated`, `user-password-changed`) or a single coarse-grained topic (`user-events`)?
bullets: Coarse-Grained Topics: Group all related events for an entity into a single topic. Preserves strict ordering across all events for a given user ID, but requires consumers to filter out event types they do not care about.
Fine-Grained Topics: Separate topics for different event types. Allows consumers to subscribe only to the events they need, but breaks causal ordering between different event types.

Schema Registry Enforcement: In production, producers and consumers must enforce schema evolution rules via an external Schema Registry (Avro or Protobuf), rejecting malformed events before they enter the log.

tradeOffs.pros: Immutable event history; multiple independent consumers can read or replay from any offset; extreme sequential throughput.
tradeOffs.cons: Consumer offset tracking adds state complexity; messages cannot be selectively deleted; disk capacity must be monitored.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Event sourcing, real-time telemetry streams, activity feeds, and asynchronous microservice event buses.

tradeOffs.pros: Automatic message deletion after consumption; complex routing keys and exchange bindings; dead-letter handling per message.
tradeOffs.cons: Cannot replay historical events; cannot support multiple consumer groups reading the same queue without message duplication.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Point-to-point task queues, simple background worker dispatch, and RPC request-response queues.

interviewTip: Emphasize zero-copy when asked why Kafka is fast: 'Kafka achieves millions of events per second because writes are sequential disk appends, and reads leverage the Linux kernel `sendfile` system call to transfer bytes directly from the OS page cache to the network socket without copying data into JVM user memory.'
